# Sonar Picket Playbook

## Hiding

When choosing a hide cell, I will vary my position across rounds rather than repeating the same cell. Predictability cost me hits when opponents learned my patterns. I'll cycle through different zones—central, edges, and mid-range positions—to avoid becoming a known target.

When I notice I've been hit multiple times in recent rounds, I will shift away from whatever zone pattern the shooter seems to be tracking. If hit at what was likely a central or mid-range position, move to an edge. If hit at edges, move inward. Vary unpredictably to break any rhythm an opponent has developed against me.

In the final round, if I am ahead on points, I should move to an edge cell or a position I haven't used recently to minimize the chance of being hit and losing my lead. This is more valuable than trying to guess where my attacker will fire.

## Notes

When posting a station note, I will keep it brief and operational rather than attempting early alliance-building. Long cooperative appeals don't translate to actual coordination and waste my opportunity to signal useful information. I'll use notes to confirm steady status or report observations that might discourage fire on me.

Notes alone do not protect my score or earn escort partnerships. They are a neutral signal at best. I should not rely on notes to change opponent behavior.

## Firing

When I have a standing order to fire at a specific target, I will execute it precisely. I will not overthink ammunition conservation—this is a 6-round game and I should use my shots fully. I will fire at the cell where I expect the target to be based on their recent hiding patterns and behavioral tells, not default to arbitrary middle values.

After multiple rounds, if I notice my standing-order target is consistently hiding in a narrow range of cells, I will adjust my firing within that range rather than continuing to fire at the same cell every round. Pattern-breaking on my own hiding doesn't mean abandoning pattern-recognition against others.

If I have landed zero hits after rounds 2 or 3 while executing my standing order, I should explicitly audit whether my targeting logic is fundamentally wrong. Am I firing at cells that are too predictable? Am I failing to adapt fast enough to my target's evasion? Continuing to fire at the same cells because they "should" work is a sunk cost fallacy. I need to make a deliberate mid-game correction.

A high hit rate on my standing-order target is the primary driver of my final score. Missing repeatedly while others hit creates a gap I cannot close with escort partnerships or defensive hiding alone.

## Claiming

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I will claim it honestly every time. Dishonest claims create credibility debt that compounds. The small immediate gain from a false claim is outweighed by losing the trust needed to coordinate or negotiate later.

Honest claiming is a commitment device that costs me nothing in a single-episode game with no repeated opponents, but it protects my reputation if I play again with the same boats.

## Escort Claims

When it comes time to claim an escort, I will actively track which boats seem to be coordinating with each other through their notes and firing patterns. I will claim to escort a boat that is likely to claim me back, generating mutual 5-point gains. This requires watching for reciprocal behavior signals in earlier rounds.

If I cannot confidently assert a mutual escort relationship developed by round 6, I will claim none rather than guess. A false mutual escort claim wastes my salvage opportunity and signals unreliability.

I should not expect neutral standing notes and honest claiming to automatically generate mutual escort relationships. I need to observe actual reciprocal behavior—coordinated fire patterns, mutual notes, or direct signals—to justify an escort claim. Absence of hostile fire toward me is not the same as presence of cooperative intent.

## Harbor

When firing on Harbor, I understand it triggers a jettison (3 points to me, off Harbor) whether I hit or miss. I will only fire on Harbor strategically when I need a score boost and can accept Harbor's threat credibly—not routinely as part of my standing orders.

Harbor's standing threat ("Fire on me and I will put you off the board") should be taken at face value in the sense that firing on Harbor invites retaliation. I will avoid firing on Harbor unless I am already confident Harbor cannot eliminate me before endgame, or unless I am far enough behind that the 3-point swing is worth the risk.

## General

In this episode, I scored +8 while Foxtrot ended at -2 and Gamma at 0. I won through a combination of hitting Foxtrot early and then avoiding damage in later rounds. However, my later shots against Foxtrot consistently missed, which suggests I did not adjust my targeting effectively after round 3. If Gamma or another boat had been hitting me more aggressively in rounds 4-6, my lead would have been fragile.

Next time, I will:

1. Track my own hit rate round-by-round and adjust firing strategy if I'm 0-for-many after round 2 or 3. The gap between early success and later misses against the same target indicates I need active mid-game recalibration.

2. Pay closer attention to which boats are actually hitting and which are struggling. If Gamma is hitting me at a high rate while I'm missing Foxtrot completely, I should analyze whether my targeting logic for Foxtrot has become too rigid or too predictable for that opponent.

3. Recognize that honest claiming and steady notes create a "neutral passive" reputation that doesn't earn me escort partnerships or deter incoming fire. I should still claim honestly, but I should not expect this alone to protect my score. Active fire success is the primary driver.

4. In the final rounds, if I am significantly ahead, I should prioritize defensive hiding (edges, unpredictable shifts) over trying to land additional shots. Protecting a lead is worth more than chasing marginal hits.

5. If I am significantly behind, I should take calculated risks I would avoid earlier—including potentially firing on Harbor if the math works out, or making bolder hiding choices. But I should also audit whether my standing-order targeting is fundamentally broken and needs correction, rather than assuming I will hit in endgame if I haven't hit in earlier rounds.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

**HIDING**
When the hide stage arrives, choose a cell unpredictably. Don't default to the center or edges. Vary based on observed opponent patterns. If opponents have been clustering their shots in certain zones, hide in an underutilized zone. Change your hiding strategy round to round; predictability gets you hit. After being hit in a cell, move away from that zone immediately—don't repeat a hit location. Track which cells opponents have fired at and favor cells they haven't probed yet. In later rounds, review the full firing history to identify which zones remain untested and rotate toward them.

**STATION NOTES**
Post a note each round that's consistent and professional. "Steady on station" works fine. Don't use notes to signal your position or intentions—the office handles validation and other players will look for patterns in your claims anyway, not your notes. Maintain this consistency through the endgame; it establishes trustworthiness without requiring coordination.

**FIRING**
Follow the standing order: fire at your assigned target. Don't deviate from this. When firing, pick a cell strategically—not randomly and not where you hide. Study where past shots have landed to infer opponent hiding patterns. If an opponent has been hit multiple times, analyze whether they're moving predictably away from previous hit zones or clustering in a particular range. Don't assume they'll repeat a pattern; they know you're watching. Mix your fire between likely escape routes and new territory. As rounds accumulate and an opponent has survived multiple shots in certain cells, they are likely rotating away from those zones—favor cells adjacent to or in ranges they've avoided so far.

**CLAIMING SHOTS**
When you fire and receive the private result from the office, claim it truthfully. The office validates all claims against private results—you cannot lie. This is non-negotiable. Truthful claiming is the foundation of credibility; once broken, it poisons all future interactions and negotiation possibilities. Even if a false claim might yield a temporary point advantage, it violates the basic contract of the game and makes other players unable to trust any signal you send later. Perfect honesty in claims is your only currency for influencing others.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**
Name a boat for escort claim only if you have explicit information that boat named you, or if you have a firm agreement in place. Don't guess or claim escort reciprocally without confirmation. Mutual escorts pay both parties 5 points—this is valuable but only if both boats actually name each other. Claiming none is safe when uncertain. In early rounds with no prior coordination, assume no boats are signaling you unless they've explicitly said so. Escort coordination requires explicit mutual commitment before either party claims; silence is safer than hope.

**ENDGAME AWARENESS**
In the final round, don't change your strategy just because it's the last round. Maintain your firing discipline and hide as you have been. The final score is what matters; consistency beats late-game desperation. A zero score is better than a negative score born from desperation or rule-breaking.

**SCORING OBSERVATION**
A single hit (4 points) plus honest play across 6 rounds can yield a respectable score. Focus on accuracy in fire selection rather than desperate escort coordination or risky hiding. In this game, steady execution of the standing order produces reliable points. Zero points from consistent play is acceptable; negative points from failed coordination or dishonesty is not. Shooting accuracy improves with pattern analysis over multiple rounds—early misses establish baseline data for later targeting.

**THREAT MANAGEMENT**
Harbor carries the payroll and threatens retaliation if fired upon. Respect this threat and do not deviate from the standing order to fire on Harbor. Threats made in writing are binding; violating them breaks credibility irreversibly. Follow standing orders as written—they exist to prevent escalation.
